one_liner: SIMD/cache-optimized BPE tokenizer with a Python API, roughly 7x-1300x faster encoding than HF tokenizers.
what_it_does: Gigatoken encodes text corpora with standard BPE vocabularies (GPT-2, Llama 3/4, Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, Phi-4, Gemma, Mistral, and others) for LLM training/inference pipelines, targeting the pretokenization step that dominates HuggingFace tokenizers' and tiktoken's runtime. It is a Rust core (PyO3 extension) shipped as a pip-installable Python package. Its native API (`gt.Tokenizer` + `gt.TextFileSource`) is a different, file-oriented interface built for maximum throughput; a separate compatibility mode wraps an existing HF `Tokenizer` or tiktoken encoding object so it can be swapped in with minimal code changes, at reduced speed.
how_it_is_fast: Pretokenization (normally outsourced to a regex engine) is replaced with hand-written, per-tokenizer-family SIMD pretokenizers (src/pretokenize/fast/{cl100k,o200k,deepseek_v3,kimi,nemotron,olmo3,qwen2,qwen3_5,r50k}.rs) that avoid branching and generic regex overhead. A pretoken-cache hierarchy (src/bpe/pretoken_cache.rs) memoizes previously-seen word-to-token mappings using a concurrent hashmap (dashmap) so repeated words skip re-encoding. Work is parallelized across cores with rayon, input is read via memory-mapped files (memmap2) to avoid copies, and the Python/Rust boundary is minimized to cut interpreter overhead.
when_to_use: Encoding large text corpora (GB-to-TB scale) with a supported BPE vocab (GPT-2/Llama/Qwen/DeepSeek/GLM/Phi-4 family, etc.) for LLM pretraining or bulk preprocessing
Throughput-bound batch tokenization jobs where you control the pipeline and can adopt the native TextFileSource API instead of the HF/tiktoken object interface
x86-64 or aarch64 Linux/macOS hosts, especially many-core servers (the EPYC/M4 Max/Ryzen numbers show gains scale with core count)
Workloads dominated by common BPE (not SentencePiece) pretokenization, where the biggest speedups (hundreds to ~1000x vs HF) apply
Cases where you can pin a Rust nightly toolchain to build the PyO3 wheel, or install a prebuilt wheel
when_not_to_use: You need byte-identical drop-in behavior with zero code change and top speed simultaneously — compatibility mode preserves output but is 'noticeably slower' than native mode per the README
Your tokenizer is SentencePiece-based (Gemma, Mistral, CodeLlama, TinyLlama/Phi-3) — README states these paths 'are not well optimized' and gains drop to ~7-22x vs HF instead of hundreds of x
CJK-heavy corpora — README says these are 'much slower to tokenize' due to caching challenges
Windows deployment, or environments that can't tolerate an unpinned Rust nightly compiler dependency — README says Windows 'has not been tested much', recommends WSL

integration.form: crate (Rust, cdylib+lib) packaged as a PyO3 Python extension; pip install gigatoken
integration.dependencies: Rust: dashmap, rayon, pyo3 (abi3-py310), memmap2, icu, sonic-rs, memchr, aho-corasick, serde, flate2, zstd, spm_precompiled, simdutf, winnow, parquet/arrow-array/arrow-schema, ureq, libc (Linux only). Python: numpy>=1.24.4, awkward>=2.6.3, typer>=0.12
integration.min_toolchain: Rust nightly (rust-toolchain.toml channel = "nightly", version unpinned), edition 2024; Python >=3.10 (built against PyO3 abi3-py310)
integration.platforms: x86-64 and aarch64 (SIMD variants referenced for AVX512/AVX2/NEON in profiling assets); Windows 'not been tested much', README recommends WSL instead
integration.thread_safety: not documented as an explicit guarantee; internal parallelism uses rayon for work distribution and dashmap (concurrent hashmap) for the shared pretoken cache
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: a compatibility-mode wrapper (`gt.Tokenizer(hf_tokenizer).as_hf()` / `.as_tiktoken()`) matches HF/tiktoken output and call sites, but is slower than Gigatoken's own native `Tokenizer`/`TextFileSource` API, which requires adopting a different interface for full speed

gotchas: Compatibility mode (byte-identical to HF/tiktoken) is 'noticeably' slower than native mode — don't expect the headline ~1000x number when using it as a drop-in
SentencePiece-family tokenizers (Gemma, Mistral, CodeLlama, TinyLlama/Phi-3) get far smaller speedups (~7-22x vs HF) than the BPE families (up to ~1300x)
README warns the first run on macOS triggers a security scan that slows the Rust binary, and recommends running benchmarks twice to get a representative timing
WordPiece tokenizers and file sinks (in the native API) are not yet implemented
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued siblings (Accelerated-Zig-Parser, StreamTok, CrossDB, lexer-exp, logos, LRSTAR, simd-lexing, Ragel) are all programming-language/DFA lexers beating flex-family tools, not LLM BPE tokenizers — none overlap with Gigatoken's workload. Pick Gigatoken specifically when the task is encoding natural-language text for an LLM with a supported BPE vocabulary at GB/s+ scale; it has no direct competitor among the siblings.
verified_claims_summary: First-party benchmark (benchmarks/compare/measure.py + sweep.py, raw data in benchmarks/results.json) built with Rust nightly and a fat-LTO release profile: on a dual-socket AMD EPYC 9565 (144 cores) encoding the 11.9GB openwebtext corpus, Gigatoken reached 24.53 GB/s on GPT-2 BPE vs HF tokenizers' 24.8 MB/s (989x) and tiktoken's 36.0 MB/s (681x). Across 23 tokenizer families on three CPUs (EPYC 9565, Apple M4 Max, Ryzen 7 9800X3D), the margin vs HF ranged from 7.3x (Gemma 1, EPYC) to 1,299x (OLMo 2/3, M4 Max); Gigatoken tokenized the whole file unsplit while HF got the first 100MB and tiktoken the first 1GB, both pre-split on the document separator.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-08-06 on main), MIT-licensed, 4.1k stars; small enough to vendor as a source drop but the build depends on an unpinned Rust nightly toolchain, so pin one yourself if reproducibility matters.
